## Parasite load and infectiousness

With $t$ being the time post drug administration and $\tau$ the time post mosquito
infection, $\alpha(t, \tau)$ and $\beta(t, \tau)$ are respectively the transmission
blocking (TBA) and reducing (TRA) activities as characterized on oocysts. Figures 2a
and 2c show data of $\alpha(t, \tau = 4\,\mbox{dpi})$ and
$\beta(t, \tau = 4\,\mbox{dpi})$ respectively.

The average reduction of parasite load in mosquitoes infected $\tau$ days ago and
biting people treated $t$ days ago can be expressed as

$$
(1 - \alpha(t, \tau))(1 - \beta(t, \tau))
$$

If $h(t)$ is the distribution of times post drug administration in the population of
treated humans, the average reduction $l(\tau)$ of parasite load in mosquitoes infected
$\tau$ days ago due to 1 bite on treated people then reads

$$
l(\tau) = \int_0^{+\infty}(1 - \alpha(t, \tau))(1 - \beta(t, \tau))h(t)dt
$$

Among mosquitoes infected $\tau$ days ago, if $\lambda(\tau)$ is the ratio of the
parasite average load expressed relative to what we would get in total absence of
treatment in the human population then

$$
\frac{d\lambda}{d\tau} = -(1 - l(\tau)) a p \lambda(\tau)
$$

with

$$
\lambda(0) = 1
$$

leading to 

$$
\lambda(\tau) = \exp\left[-ap\int_0^\tau(1 - l(u))du\right]
$$

where $p$ is the proportion of humans who received treatment and $a$ is the mosquito
biting rate. If $f$ is the relationship between the parasite load and the mosquito
infectiousness, then the reduction factor of infectiousness due to TBA and TRA reads:

$$
\rho = \int_0^{+\infty}e^{-g\tau}f(\lambda(\tau))d\tau
$$

where $g$ is the mosquito death rate.

## Parasite development and EIP

Let's now work out the extension of the EIP. The EIP is the time at which the parasite
reaches maturity and a good proxy of maturity is the oocyst size. Oocyst size increases
as a function of time post infection $\tau$ at a rate $\nu$ that is independent of the
oocyst size itself (REF). Let's define the instrumental variable $z$ that captures the
level of maturity with

$$
z(\tau = 0) = 0
$$
$$
z(\tau = \mbox{EPI}) = 1
$$

and 

$$
\frac{dz}{d\tau} = \nu(\tau)
$$
where the rate of maturation, if independent of the state of maturation, can still
depend on the time post infection $\tau$. Let's now introduce $\delta(t, \tau)$ the
reduction factor of the rate of parasite development for a mosquito getting 1 blood
meal at time $\tau$ post infection on a human host who is at time $t$ post treatment.
The average reduction $q(\tau)$ of the parasite development rate in mosquitoes at time
$\tau$ post infection due to 1 bite on treated people then reads

$$
q(\tau) = \int_0^{+\infty} \delta(t, \tau) h(t) dt
$$

Taking into account the proportion $p$ of humans taking treatment and the mosquito
biting rate $a$, the dependency of $\nu$ on $\tau$ is governed by

$$
\frac{d\nu}{d\tau} = (q(\tau) - 1)ap\nu
$$
with 

$$
\nu(0) = \frac{1}{n}
$$

leading to

$$
\nu(\tau) = \frac{1}{n} \exp\left[ap\int_0^{\tau}(q(u) - 1)du\right]
$$

where $n$ is the value of the EIP in absence of treatment in the human population. Now
that we have this, we can implicitly express the average EIP $T$ in presence of the
treatment in the human population as the solution of

$$
\int_0^{T}\nu(\tau)d\tau = 1
$$

## $R_0$ reduction effect

Putting previous results together, if $R_0$ is the value of the basic reproduction
number in absence of treatment, then, in the presence of treatment in the population,
its expression becomes

$$
\rho e^{(n - T)g} R_0
$$
